Axillary wrasse Symphodus mediterraneus exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a value that places it among the medium-sized labrids inhabiting Mediterranean seagrass meadows. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain sexual maturity upon reaching approximately 9 cm [Lp = approximately 9 cm] in total length, corresponding to the onset of gonadal development and the transition to reproductive competency. This length at puberty falls within the typical range of 7 to 10 cm observed across related species, suggesting a conserved size threshold for reproductive activation in this genus. The relationship between length and mass follows a power function derived from conspecifics, yielding an estimated ultimate wet weight of 67.8 grams [Wwi = 67.8 grams] for adults that have achieved their asymptotic size. Such body mass is consistent with the energetic demands of nesting and parental care behaviours characteristic of this species.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at approximately 16% [GSI = approximately 16%] for this wrasse at a water temperature of 10.7 °C [T = 10.7 °C]. This value, which draws on comparative data from the closely related Symphodus melops, reflects a moderate allocation of somatic resources toward gamete production during the spawning season. At the temperature threshold specified, metabolic rates and vitellogenic processes are likely optimised to support the energetic costs associated with oocyte maturation and repeated spawning events. The index provides a useful gauge for assessing how thermal regimes influence reproductive effort in small-bodied labrids, particularly those inhabiting the variable thermal environments of coastal Mediterranean waters.

Larval development in Symphodus mediterraneus begins with the production of small, pelagic eggs from which hatchlings emerge at a remarkably low wet weight of 0.00039 grams [Wwb = 0.00039 grams]. This initial mass, derived from an assumed egg diameter and spherical volume calculation, underscores the extreme metabolic vulnerability characteristic of marine teleost larvae. Newly hatched individuals rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase, as the mouth is not yet functional and the digestive tract remains undifferentiated. The transition to exogenous feeding involves a critical period during which first prey capture must occur before energy reserves are exhausted, making larval survival heavily dependent on the spatial and temporal availability of suitable planktonic prey. Field studies indicate that growth during this period is rapid but highly variable.

Individuals that successfully navigate the larval phase and recruit to benthic habitats undergo a period of somatic growth leading to reproductive maturation. At the length of puberty, 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm], the corresponding wet weight is approximately 8.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.1 grams], a value derived from the same length-mass relationship that characterises the population. This mass marks the threshold at which energy resources are considered sufficient to support the costs of gametogenesis and nesting behaviour. Comparisons among Mediterranean labrids suggest that the mass at puberty is tightly linked to the energetic demands of male nest construction and egg fanning, as well as female egg production. The relatively modest body size at maturation aligns with an opportunistic life-history strategy, allowing individuals to begin reproducing within their first or second year.

The maximum lifespan of Symphodus mediterraneus has been estimated at 2920 days [am = 2920 days] under ambient thermal conditions averaging 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately eight years, is typical for a labrid of its body size and reflects the trade-off between early reproductive output and sustained somatic maintenance. Older individuals frequently exhibit reduced spawning frequency and slower fin regeneration rates, consistent with the onset of reproductive senescence. The species' iteroparous life cycle, combined with a multiyear reproductive window, allows for compensatory reproduction in years of poor recruitment. Understanding these demographic parameters is essential for assessing population resilience in the face of ongoing climate-driven warming of Mediterranean coastal waters.
